summary: I reviewed the dvpwa aiohttp application: DAO layer (SQL queries), views/routes, auth utilities, middlewares, app bootstrap, Jinja2 templates/processors, config schema and fixtures. Overall risk is critical. There is an unauthenticated SQL injection in student creation, and the app globally disables HTML auto-escaping producing stored XSS. Supporting weaknesses (unsalted MD5 passwords, disabled CSRF middleware, non-HttpOnly session cookies, missing authorization on state-changing endpoints, and framework debug mode) compound the impact. Static assets and CSS/JS libraries were not audited.

findings.title: SQL injection in Student.create via unsanitized name
findings.description: Student.create builds an INSERT statement by interpolating the student name directly into the SQL string with Python %-formatting, then executes it with no parameters. The name is fully attacker-controlled: the students view (sqli/views.py:54-57) reads data['name'] from an unauthenticated POST /students/ request and passes it straight to Student.create. Because the CSRF middleware is disabled (sqli/app.py:27) and the view has no @authorize decorator, any anonymous user can inject arbitrary SQL. A payload in the name field (e.g. closing the quote and appending stacked queries or a sub-select) allows reading other tables such as users.pwd_hash, or modifying/deleting data. This is the classic sink; every other DAO method correctly uses bound parameters.
findings.evidence:
q = ("INSERT INTO students (name) "
     "VALUES ('%(name)s')" % {'name': name})
... await cur.execute(q)  # no params

Source: views.py students(): data = await request.post(); await Student.create(conn, data['name'])
findings.recommendation: Use a parameterized query exactly like the other DAOs: q = "INSERT INTO students (name) VALUES (%(name)s)"; await cur.execute(q, {'name': name}). Never interpolate user input into SQL text.

findings.title: Stored XSS from globally disabled Jinja2 autoescape
findings.description: aiohttp_jinja2 is configured with autoescape=False, so no template output is HTML-escaped. Multiple templates render user-controlled, persisted data verbatim: course.jinja2:22 outputs review.review_text, course.jinja2:14-15 outputs course.title/description, students.jinja2:16 outputs student names. Course reviews are created via POST /courses/{id}/review (views.py:111-131) with no authentication and no output encoding, and review_text has no sanitization (schema only checks min_length). An attacker submits a review containing <script>... which is stored and then executed in the browser of every visitor to that course page, including the superadmin — enabling session/cookie theft (see the non-HttpOnly cookie finding) and admin actions.
findings.evidence:
setup_jinja(app, loader=PackageLoader('sqli','templates'), context_processors=[...], autoescape=False)

course.jinja2:22  {{ review.review_text }}   # rendered without escaping
Review.create stores review_text unmodified (dao/review.py:28-36)
findings.recommendation: Enable autoescaping: pass autoescape=jinja2.select_autoescape(['html','jinja2']) (or autoescape=True) to setup_jinja, and use |safe only for values known to be safe. Optionally validate/sanitize review_text on input.

findings.title: Passwords hashed with unsalted MD5
findings.description: User.check_password compares the stored hash to md5(password) with no salt and no work factor; the fixtures likewise store md5('superadmin') etc. (migrations/001-fixtures.sql:10-13). MD5 is fast and unsalted, so if the users table is disclosed (e.g. via the SQL injection above) the password hashes fall instantly to rainbow tables/brute force, exposing the superadmin account. This is the storage/verification sink.
findings.evidence:
return self.pwd_hash == md5(password.encode('utf-8')).hexdigest()
Fixtures: md5('superadmin'), md5('password')
findings.recommendation: Use a slow, salted password hash such as bcrypt, scrypt or argon2 (e.g. passlib/argon2-cffi), and rehash existing credentials on next login.

findings.title: CSRF protection disabled (csrf_middleware commented out)
findings.description: The csrf_middleware that validates a per-session _csrf_token on POST requests (defined in sqli/middlewares.py:25-38) is commented out of the middleware list, so no CSRF check runs for any state-changing POST endpoint (login, create student, create course, submit review, evaluate, logout). Although templates still emit a _csrf_token hidden field, it is never verified. A malicious page can force a logged-in admin's browser to submit forms (e.g. evaluate students, create records) cross-site.
findings.recommendation: Re-enable csrf_middleware in the middleware chain so the token comparison in middlewares.py runs for all POST requests.

findings.title: Session cookie set with HttpOnly disabled
findings.description: The session storage is created with RedisStorage(app['redis'], httponly=False), so the session cookie is readable by client-side JavaScript. Combined with the stored XSS (disabled autoescape) this lets an injected script exfiltrate the session cookie via document.cookie and hijack an authenticated/admin session. The cookie is also not marked Secure.
findings.recommendation: Remove httponly=False (default is HttpOnly) and set secure=True so the session cookie cannot be read by JavaScript and is only sent over HTTPS.

findings.title: Missing authorization on state-changing endpoints (evaluate, student/course creation)
findings.description: The evaluate handler creates a Mark for a student with no authentication or admin check, even though the UI exposes this action only to admins (course.jinja2:41 gates the form on auth_user.is_admin). Any anonymous user can POST /students/{id}/evaluate/{course_id} to assign grades. The same missing-authorization pattern applies to POST /students/ (views.py:54-57) and POST /courses/ (views.py:86-90), which mutate data without any @authorize decorator; only logout is decorated. The root cause is the absence of authorization enforcement on these handlers.
findings.evidence:
async def evaluate(request): ... await Mark.create(conn, student_id, course_id, data['points'])  # no get_auth_user / @authorize
Compare authorize() decorator in utils/auth.py used only on logout.
findings.recommendation: Apply the existing @authorize(ensure_admin=True) decorator to evaluate and @authorize() to the create/mutating handlers, enforcing authentication/role checks server-side rather than only in templates.

findings.title: aiohttp application runs with debug mode enabled
findings.description: The Application is constructed with debug=True, which enables verbose diagnostics and detailed error reporting. In production this can leak stack traces and internal details useful to an attacker. It is hardcoded rather than driven from configuration/environment.
findings.recommendation: Drive debug from configuration/environment and default it to False in production deployments.
